changes.before: The threshold rises while every score stays fixed. Did the model necessarily retrain?
changes.after: A threshold turns a score into a decision without necessarily changing the model.

before: A classifier may output a score before the application makes a yes-or-no decision. A threshold converts that score into an action under an explicit rule.
Suppose the rule is predict positive when score is at least 0.6. Scores 0.4 and 0.59 are negative; 0.6 and 0.8 are positive. The equality rule matters at the boundary.
Worked example: with unchanged scores 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8, raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.7 reduces positive predictions from two to one. No model weights changed in this comparison.

A threshold changes which cases receive a positive decision. To assess the consequences, compare against known labels and count false positives and false negatives. A score is not automatically a well-calibrated probability.
Changed situation: The threshold rises while every score stays fixed. Did the model necessarily retrain?
The same model scores can be interpreted using a different decision threshold.
after: A classifier can produce a score before an app makes a yes-or-no decision. A threshold is the cutoff used for that decision.
Our rule says positive when the score is at least the threshold. At least includes equality: a score exactly on the cutoff counts as positive.
The scores stayed the same. This example changed only the decision rule; it did not train a model or change its weights.
Compare the new decisions with known answers. Count false positives and false negatives to see the effect of the new cutoff.
A probability estimates how likely something is. A model's score is not automatically a reliable probability. That interpretation needs its own checks.
